analysis.investment_thesis: Aavas Financiers has built an impressive 7-year track record of 29.7% net profit CAGR and 22% revenue CAGR serving rural/semi-urban first-time homebuyers — a segment that big banks chronically ignore. However, FY25 revenue actually dipped (INR 2,018 Cr → 1,988 Cr), which raises a caution flag that the growth story may be decelerating.
key_strengths: Outstanding long-run earnings compounding: net profit grew from INR 93 Cr (FY18) to INR 574 Cr (FY25) at 29.7% CAGR, making P/E 21.8x look cheap — PEG ~0.73
Focused niche: semi-urban and rural affordable housing in Rajasthan and contiguous states, with strong relationship-based underwriting that keeps NIMs healthy
High institutional confidence: FIIs own 24.72% and DIIs own 14.30%, suggesting sophisticated investors have already done diligence on asset quality
key_risks: Revenue declined in FY25 (INR 2,018 Cr → 1,988 Cr) — the first contraction in 7 years of data — this is the key watch item that could downgrade this to AVOID
D/E of 3.08 is the highest of the HFCs in this peer group, leaving less buffer for credit stress
Geographic concentration in semi-urban Rajasthan and nearby states limits diversification and increases regional economic risk
red_flags: FY25 revenue declined for the first time in the data series — if this is a trend rather than an anomaly, the 29.7% CAGR story is over
Finance cost data for FY25 shows INR 5 Cr (vs INR 828 Cr in FY24) — likely a reclassification or data error, obscuring true cost of funds
analysis.detailed_analysis: Aavas is the kind of company Lynch calls a 'fast grower in a niche that nobody's watching' — rural housing finance for informal-income earners using on-ground verification rather than credit bureaus. The 7-year earnings CAGR of 29.7% with a P/E of 21.8 gives a PEG of 0.73, which is genuinely attractive. Management has consistently grown the loan book (assets from INR 7,657 Cr to INR 18,618 Cr over 5 years) while maintaining profitability. The negative OCF (-1,660 Cr in FY25) is structural for any HFC — loans disbursed are 'operating outflows' — and not a concern in isolation.
